description: Itzpapalotl, whose name translates to "Obsidian Butterfly" or "Clawed Butterfly," is a prominent and complex figure in Aztec mythology. She is a fearsome skeletal goddess, often depicted with obsidian or flint knives on her wings. Itzpapalotl embodies the duality of life and death, representing both the destructive and regenerative aspects of the natural world. She is associated with the Tzitzimime, star demons who threatened to devour humanity during solar eclipses. While fearsome, she also held connections to agriculture and fertility, highlighting the cyclical nature of existence. Her influence extended to the realm of the sacred calendar and divinatory practices.
shortDescription: Itzpapalotl is a fearsome skeletal goddess in Aztec mythology, associated with death, agriculture, and the transformative power of the earth.

subtitle: Obsidian Butterfly: Death and Rebirth
appearance: Itzpapalotl is typically depicted as a skeletal figure adorned with butterfly wings edged with obsidian blades. Her face is often a skull, and she may be shown wearing jaguar claws. The obsidian blades represent her power to cut life short, while the butterfly wings symbolize transformation and rebirth.

extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: Itzpapalotl's origins are somewhat obscure, but she is believed to predate the Aztec civilization, possibly stemming from earlier Mesoamerican cultures. In Aztec mythology, she is associated with the Tzitzimime, celestial beings who emerged during periods of cosmic instability. Itzpapalotl is sometimes considered their leader or a powerful member of their ranks. Myths often depict her as a warrior goddess, involved in battles and possessing immense power. She appears in various codices, including the Codex Borgia, where her iconography and associations are detailed. One notable myth involves her role in the creation or destruction of humanity during different cosmic ages.

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: Itzpapalotl played a multifaceted role in Aztec religion and society. As a goddess of death and destruction, she was feared and respected. Her association with the Tzitzimime made her a figure to be appeased, particularly during eclipses, to prevent cosmic chaos. However, she also held significance in agriculture, representing the transformative power of the earth to both destroy and regenerate life. This duality made her a complex deity, embodying the cyclical nature of existence. Her influence extended to divination and the sacred calendar, where her days were often considered unfavorable.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: Itzpapalotl's symbolism is rich and layered. The obsidian butterfly represents the sharp, cutting edge of death, as well as the transformative process of metamorphosis. Her skeletal form emphasizes the impermanence of life and the inevitability of death. The jaguar claws signify her warrior nature and power. As a deity linked to both death and agriculture, she embodies the cyclical nature of life, death, and rebirth. Her association with the Tzitzimime highlights the ever-present threat of cosmic chaos and the need for balance in the universe. She can be interpreted as a reminder of the fragility of existence and the constant interplay between creation and destruction.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: While the Aztec civilization was conquered centuries ago, Itzpapalotl continues to hold a place in contemporary culture. She is a symbol of female power and resilience. Her image is sometimes used in art and literature to represent the duality of nature and the cyclical nature of life. Contemporary artists and writers draw inspiration from her complex symbolism, exploring themes of death, rebirth, and transformation. She is also a figure of interest in neopagan and indigenous spiritual practices that seek to reconnect with pre-Columbian traditions. Her image can be found in modern interpretations of Aztec art and mythology, demonstrating her enduring legacy.
